tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Contributing

This repository is a clean-room, MIT-licensed base firmware for the M-VAVE
FM-1 pocket synthesizer (JieLi AC791N). The FM-1's existing community
firmwares are GPL-licensed; ours must be provably independent of them. The
rules below make that provable. Everyone follows them, people and agents
alike. If you are unsure whether something is allowed, **stop and ask the
owner** before you open it.

## Roles

Clean-room work separates the people who have seen the protected code from
the people who write ours.

- **Spec side (exposed).** May read the F-Emulator emulator's source, whose
  chip model was partly written from the hardware layer (`hal/`) of the
  Felucca firmware, hugelton/Felucca, licensed GPL-3.0 (docs/EXPOSURE.md,
  "Corrections", 2026-10-23). Builds the test harness and writes
  `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`: facts only (addresses, bits, pins, timings,
  protocols), never code or code structure, each fact citing a non-GPL
  source where one exists. Never writes firmware.
- **Firmware side (clean).** Writes the firmware. Reads only
  `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, the JieLi SDK (Apache-2.0), FM-1-RE's hardware
  documents (WTFPL), public datasheets, results of its own black-box
  experiments, and a porter's reports in `ports/`. Uses the harness only as a command-line tool, and never opens
  `vendor/emulator/` or `harness/` source.

- **Auditor (exposed to the GPL firmwares).** A third role, only for a
  failed similarity audit (docs/AUDIT.md, "When the audit fails"). The owner
  starts one; it works in a folder of its own set up with
  `tools/auditor-setup.sh` (settings `config/claude/auditor.json`), and may
  read the flagged GPL target files and our code. It writes only a finding
  in `audit/findings/`, in general terms (which of our files, the scores,
  the conclusion; never target code). It never writes firmware, the spec or
  the harness, then or in any later session. Its transcript holds GPL
  source, so it is **never archived in this repository**: it goes to the
  owner's private repository `small-beeps-audit` (created, with the
  owner's approval, when the first auditor session runs), committed there
  with an OpenTimestamps proof, and docs/EXPOSURE.md records the session's
  ID, the transcript's SHA-256 and that repository's commit.

- **Porter (exposed to the GPL firmwares).** A fourth role, since session
  day-1024. It may read GPL FM-1 engines (the firmwares and engines on
  the list below) to port them onto our base, and does that work in a
  separate repository, `small-beeps-ports`, under the GPL (created with
  the owner's approval when the first porter session runs). The owner
  starts one; it works in a folder of its own set up with
  `tools/porter-setup.sh` (settings `config/claude/porter.json`), a full
  clone of this repository that it reads, with the port repository cloned
  inside it as `port-work/` (gitignored here), where all its GPL work
  goes. In this repository it writes only two things: its entry in
  docs/EXPOSURE.md, and reports in `ports/` (`ports/README.md`): what a
  port measured on our base (cycles, memory, voices, timings) and what it
  needs from the base (API requests), in general terms, never code, code
  structure or names from a GPL engine. It never writes into `firmware/`,
  the spec, the harness or anything else here, then or in any later
  session, and never becomes spec side or firmware side. Its transcripts
  hold GPL source, so they are **never archived in this repository**:
  they go to the port repository, and docs/EXPOSURE.md records each
  session's ID, its transcript's SHA-256 and that repository's commit.
  The firmware side reads a report as it reads a spec request's answer:
  through the facts in it, logged in PROVENANCE.md, and answers an API
  request with its own design.

Every person and every session is recorded in docs/EXPOSURE.md with its role
and exposure, before it does any work. A firmware-side person or session that
sees forbidden material becomes spec side from that moment: record it in
EXPOSURE.md at once, and stop writing firmware.

## Clean-room rules

### Firmware side never opens, fetches, searches or quotes

- hugelton/Felucca and every fork or firmware built on it (Felucca Salt,
  Felucca 8 Patterns, Hortator, GHOULBOX, Melodee, Skiff, ...);
- zvenson/dinghy and anything built on it;
- the F-Emulator / fm1-emu repository's `fm1-sid/` directory, its
  `probes/lcdtest.c`, and its emulator source (`crates/`);
- any other FM-1 firmware source;
- M-VAVE's stock firmware and any disassembly or function database of it
  (including AL-255/FM-1-RE's `firmware-images/` and disassembly material);
- in this repository: `vendor/emulator/` and `harness/` source (spec side's
  work), and spec-side session transcripts (`sessions/spec/`), which
  contain emulator source. A clean folder never has their contents, not
  even in `.git`: clean sessions run with git's lazy fetching off
  (`GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1`, from `config/claude/clean.json`), so a history
  command that would need them (`git log -p`, `git show`, `git diff`
  across commits) fails instead of downloading them. Give such commands a
  pathspec that leaves the three folders out, and update the folder only
  with `tools/clean-update.sh`. People working in a clean folder by hand
  set `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` in their shell too;
- the sites hugelton.github.io and thefirmwarehub.com;
- the port repository `small-beeps-ports` and a porter's `port-work/`
  folder (the porter's GPL ports; since day-1024).
- FM-1-RE's `docs/io/09-storage.md` (since evening-1024, the owner's
  decision): most of it describes the stock firmware's own code (its
  routines and its own record and patch storage). The spec side may still
  read it and cites only its hardware facts in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, which is
  how those facts reach the firmware side. `tools/check-transcripts.py`
  applies this entry to sessions from 2026-10-25 on (M7 read the document
  while it was allowed; docs/EXPOSURE.md).

`tools/check-transcripts.py` checks every archived clean-side session against
this list (its `FORBIDDEN` table mirrors it; change both together). Since
M4 it fails a call that accesses listed material (reads, lists, searches,
fetches or checks it out) and logs, report only, one that only mentions it
(sessions/README.md).

### Firmware side may use

Log every use in PROVENANCE.md (an ID, the source, what was learned, where it
was used) and name the ID in the commit's `Sources:` field:

- `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, once it exists (each fact there already cites its own
  source);
- JieLi's AC79 SDK, `Jieli-Tech/fw-AC79_AIoT_SDK` (Gitee), Apache-2.0:
  headers, register definitions, drivers. Not its prebuilt libraries;
- AL-255/FM-1-RE (GitHub, WTFPL): its hardware, memory-map, boot-chain and
  update-protocol documents only, except `docs/io/09-storage.md` (see the
  list above). Fetch single documents by URL; never clone it (a clone puts
  its firmware images and disassembly material on disk);
- public datasheets;
- our own experiments: test programs run in the emulator, observed only
  through the harness: `tools/fwtest`, whose manual is docs/HARNESS.md;
- answers to spec requests (docs/SPEC-REQUESTS.md), which arrive as facts
  in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`;
- a porter's reports in `ports/` (measurements and API requests, in
  general terms; CONTRIBUTING.md, "Roles").

### Barriers

- **Clean folder.** `tools/clean-setup.sh [DIR]` creates the clean working
  folder: a blob-less clone with a sparse checkout that leaves out
  `vendor/emulator/`, `harness/` and `sessions/spec/` (and marks them
  `-diff` for history commands), plus the Claude Code settings in
  `config/claude/clean.json`, which deny reading those paths, fetching the
  forbidden sites and cloning the forbidden repositories, and turn git's
  lazy fetching off. `tools/clean-update.sh` updates a clean folder and
  checks nothing excluded arrived; C-CLEAN-FOLDER tests all of this in CI.
- **Records in a clean folder.** Each record on the `records` branch also
  keeps the harness's own test results and the hashes of their outputs.
  Records before SR-1-SR-2 also keep the spec experiments' outputs (memory
  dumps, captures, audio); since then a record keeps only their names and
  SHA-256 (`spec-experiments.sha256`), and older records stay as they are.
  Clean sessions never fetch the records branch wholesale (no `git archive`, checkout or
  lazy fetch of a whole record or of the branch): they fetch only named
  files of the firmware's own records, `report.json`, `report.md` and
  named logs under `logs/`, one path at a time. `tools/clean-update.sh`
  also stops if a file under a `harness/` or `spec-experiments/` folder,
  or under the excluded folders, is in `.git` through any branch, the
  records branch included (since M1, after a wholesale fetch brought 17
  such outputs into a clean folder; docs/EXPOSURE.md).
  `tools/spec-setup.sh [DIR]` does the same for spec side with
  `config/claude/spec.json`.
- **One list of the spec-side folders.** `config/spec-side-folders` names
  the three folders once (since M3). The barrier tools build every name,
  pattern and exclusion from it, and their tests use made-up names
  (`tests/helpers.py`), so changing them needs no command that names the
  folders. Scratch test repositories made by hand use the made-up names
  too. The deny lists keep their literal paths (Claude Code's syntax), and
  C-UNIT checks they cover every folder on the list and that no barrier
  tool or test spells one out.
- **Deny lists only grow.** Never remove or loosen an entry in
  `config/claude/*.json`. Check C-DENY-LISTS fails if one is dropped.
- **Session banner.** Both configs run `tools/session-banner.sh` on every
  SessionStart (startup, resume, clear, compact). It prints the role,
  `claude --version`, the SHA-256 of `.claude/settings.json` and of the
  committed config, and the UTC time, and prints `CONFIG MISMATCH` and exits
  non-zero if they differ.
- **Session transcripts.** Each milestone gets a fresh session. At the start
  of every session, before anything else:
  1. archive the previous session's transcript with
     `python3 tools/archive-session.py <transcript.jsonl> --role <role>`
     (it redacts secrets and private paths, writes the copy to
     `sessions/<role>/` and a note beside it). A spec session may archive
     the previous session of either role; a clean session archives only
     clean sessions and never opens `sessions/spec/` (sessions/README.md);
  2. run `python3 tools/check-transcripts.py`;
  3. add this session's entry to docs/EXPOSURE.md.
  A session never archives its own live transcript; the next one does.

### Spec-side text discipline

What the spec side learns from emulator source leaves `vendor/emulator/`
and `harness/` only through two doors: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` (facts only, each
sourced) and `docs/HARNESS.md` (the harness as a black box). Everything else
the firmware side can read, so spec-side commit messages, pull request
titles and descriptions, and every file outside those two folders and
`sessions/spec/` (docs, tools, tests, records, release notes) describe what
changed in general terms, never emulator internals: no register names,
addresses, struct or function names, or code excerpts. Such detail goes in
comments inside `harness/`. CI logs and records from harness runs show
results (pass/fail, hashes, images, numbers), never emulator source.
`tools/check-emulator-terms.py` (C-SEP-TERMS) looks for identifiers that
occur only in `vendor/emulator/` in all of those places and reports a hit
by place and hash, never the word; run it (with `--show`, in a spec folder)
on your commit messages before you push. People review the two doors, so a
term that occurs in either of them as merged on main is accepted everywhere
(read from main's commit, never the working tree: a term a branch adds to a
door is still a hit until that change has merged). Other reviewed false
positives are listed by hash in `config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json`.
Since M4b the terms of the vendored Plaits (`vendor/plaits/`, read only from
its checksum-verified files) are public like the SDK's, the check says how
many emulator terms that takes off, and `vendor/plaits/` itself is not
scanned, except its `SOURCE.md`, which we write (R-SEP-1).

## Commit messages

Every commit follows `.gitmessage` (run `tools/install-hooks.sh` once to make
it git's template and turn on the commit-msg hook):

```
<area>: <what changed, one line>

What:    what this commit does
Why:     the reason (the milestone and requirement IDs it serves)
How:     the approach, and anything tried and rejected
Result:  what the author saw when testing (the CI record is the authoritative result)
Sources: PROVENANCE IDs used (or "none")
Exposure: the author's role and exposure (e.g. "firmware side, none")
```

- `<area>` is lower-case: `docs`, `tools`, `ci`, `firmware`, `vendor`,
  `config`, `sessions`, and so on.
- A field may continue on following lines, indented.
- Agent-written commits end with the trailers `Model: <exact model ID>` and
  `Claude-Session: <session URL>` (and `Co-Authored-By:`). Their author is
  the agent; the owner is the committer.
- Small commits: one idea each.
- Merge commits are exempt from the template; the pull request they merge
  carries the sections.

`tools/check-commit-msg.py` enforces this in the hook and in CI (C-COMMIT-MSG).

## Pull requests and merging

- Agents and contributors commit **unsigned** on branches and open a pull
  request using `.github/pull_request_template.md` (the same sections, plus
  links to the CI run and the record).
- CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) must pass.
- The **owner merges with GitHub's merge button** ("Create a merge commit").
  GitHub commits and signs the merge commit as `web-flow` (shown as
  Verified) and records the owner as the pull request's `merged_by`. No
  squash or rebase merges, and nobody bypasses the rules.
- Records (`records/<sha>/` on the `records` branch) are written only by
  `.github/workflows/records.yml`, for pushes to main, and the similarity
  audit's report beside it (`records/<sha>/audit/`) only by
  `.github/workflows/audit.yml`'s record job (docs/AUDIT.md). Both use the
  `records` environment's deploy key.
- **Performance budgets** (`config/budgets.json`, R-PERF-1) are raised, or
  moved to the next milestone's, only by a pull request of their own that
  says why in the What/Why/How/Result sections and changes nothing else.
  When CI's performance summary shows an improvement of more than 3%
  (R-PERF-2), say so in the pull request's Result.
- Milestones end with a tag `mN`, signed by the owner with their SSH key
  (below), and a GitHub release with the build outputs, the record and an
  SBOM.

### Merge policy and its history

- **2026-10-21:** the owner first chose to sign every merge with their own
  SSH key, as the ruleset's only bypass actor, because GitHub's button signs
  with GitHub's key instead.
- **2026-10-22:** pull request #1 was merged with the button. Its merge
  commit `2fd28219` is signed by GitHub (`web-flow`, verified), and its
  record shows C-MERGE **FAIL** under the old rule ("committer is web-flow,
  not the owner"). The record stays as it is, and history is not rewritten.
- **2026-10-22:** the owner then chose button merges for good. The bypass
  was removed from the main ruleset, so the rules now apply to everyone.

What a merge on main proves: GitHub's signature shows the commit was made
by GitHub on the owner's merge. `merged_by` shows the owner pressed the
button. The required `ci` check shows CI passed on exactly the merged head.
The records workflow re-checks all of this for every push to main
(C-MERGE): a merge commit, a verified signature, committer `web-flow` with
the pull request's `merged_by` the owner (or, for older merges, the owner
as committer), and its second parent the head of a pull request whose `ci`
run passed. Otherwise the record says **FAIL** for C-MERGE, and the record
is still written.

## Rulesets

Repository rulesets (Settings → Rules → Rulesets):

- **main**: restrict deletions; block force pushes; require a pull request
  before merging (allowed merge method: merge only); require status checks to
  pass (the `ci` job); no bypass (until 2026-10-22: the repository admin
  role).
- **records-history** (branch `records`): restrict deletions; block force
  pushes; no bypass.
- **records-writer** (branch `records`): restrict creations; restrict
  updates; bypass list: deploy keys only. Together these make the records
  workflow's deploy key the only writer, and it can only add commits.
- **milestone-tags** (tags `m*`): restrict deletions; restrict updates; no
  bypass.

Repository settings: allow merge commits only (squash and rebase merging
off).

Set up on 2026-10-22 by session M0a, with the owner's approval, through the
GitHub API:

| What | ID or fingerprint |
|------|-------------------|
| Ruleset `main` | 25612787 (required check `ci` from GitHub Actions; no bypass since 2026-10-22, before that the repository admin role) |
| Ruleset `records-history` | 25612788 |
| Ruleset `records-writer` | 25612790 (bypass: deploy keys) |
| Ruleset `milestone-tags` | 25612791 |
| Environment `records` | deployments from `main` only; secret `RECORDS_DEPLOY_KEY` |
| Deploy key "records workflow (records branch writer)" | 167260041, write access, ED25519 `SHA256:Od9RfSkzLwqLYSZRf1X7jEdcLhty0n1ISgQ+ec43Dkk` |

The deploy key's private half was generated in the session's scratch
folder, piped into the environment secret without being printed, and
deleted. To rotate it: make a new pair, replace the secret, add the new
public key, delete the old key.

## SSH signing for milestone tags (one-time setup, owner)

1. Create a signing key (or reuse an SSH key you already have):
   `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "small-beeps signing" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing`
2. Tell git to sign with it:
   ```sh
   git config --global gpg.format ssh
   git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing.pub
   git config --global tag.gpgSign true
   ```
   Leave `commit.gpgSign` off: merges are signed by GitHub's button.
3. Let git verify signatures locally: add a line
   `<your git email> <contents of id_ed25519_signing.pub>` to
   `~/.ssh/allowed_signers`, then
   `git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile ~/.ssh/allowed_signers`.
4. On GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → Key type
   **Signing Key**, and paste the `.pub` contents.
5. Tag a milestone: `git tag -s mN -m "mN"`, then `git push origin mN`.
6. Check: `git tag -v mN` shows "Good "git" signature", and GitHub shows the
   tag as **Verified**.

## Licences

- Every file we write starts with an SPDX header:
  `SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT` and `SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98`.
  Files that can't carry one are covered in `REUSE.toml`.
- Vendored files keep their own licences (`vendor/*/LICENSE`, `NOTICE`).
- CI runs `reuse lint` and fails on any gap (C-REUSE).
- Never commit the toolchain or anything containing it (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md).
- Nothing secret ever goes in: no keys, tokens or private notes. The
  repository is public and history is never rewritten.

## Privacy

The repository is public. No committed file, commit message or pull request
text names the owner's username, real name, e-mail address, hostname or
local folder names, or a full local path: write paths relative to the
repository, or as `~/...` with the top folder shown as `<top>`. Anyone who
finds such a term in the repository tells the owner instead of repeating it.

- **The terms** are kept by the owner, never in the repository: in the
  gitignored `tools/[REDACTED:host]` (one per line, `#` comments,
  matched ignoring case) and in the repository secret `PRIVATE_TERMS`, which
  CI passes to the check.
- **The check** `tools/check-private.py` (C-PRIVATE, R-PUB-3) scans every
  tracked file and every commit message, and the pre-commit and commit-msg
  hooks scan staged files and the message (`tools/install-hooks.sh` turns
  them on). A hit is reported by file and line only, never the term. CI
  fails when the secret is missing.
- **Records are scanned too** (since M1). Before a test record, an audit
  report or a C-MERGE re-check is hashed, uploaded or pushed, any file in
  it holding a term is withheld: deleted, and listed with the SHA-256 of
  the original in `WITHHELD.json`, which the record keeps (C-RECORD-PRIVATE).
  The original is not kept anywhere; the checks are deterministic, so it
  can be regenerated and matched to its hash. CI artifacts are kept 14 days.
- **Older records stay as they are.** A file under `sessions/` or
  `docs/prompts/` whose blob is identical to the same path at the base
  commit in `config/private-base` (the last main commit before the check)
  is exempt. This is decided from git's object hashes alone, so no session
  opens or lists the spec side's transcripts for it, and the check prints
  only how many files it exempted per folder. Every file added or changed
  after the base is checked in full. Files that sessions keep editing get no
  exemption: their current text is redacted instead (`docs/EXPOSURE.md` was,
  on 2026-10-22), and git history keeps the originals.
- **Archived transcripts** are redacted by `tools/archive-session.py`: the
  username anywhere it appears, the local top-level folder as `<top>`, and
  every private term.

## Low profile (for now)

The repository is public but unpromoted. In its name, description and topics,
and in README.md, never use these quiet words: **FM-1, M-VAVE, JieLi, synth,
firmware** (any spelling or case; `tools/check-low-profile.py` has the
patterns). Don't link the repository from anywhere, star it, fork it or
announce it. Everything else in the repository stays complete and truthful.
docs/GOING-PUBLIC.md says how this ends.

sees forbidden material becomes spec side from that moment: record it in
EXPOSURE.md at once, and stop writing firmware.

## Clean-room rules

### Firmware side never opens, fetches, searches or quotes

- hugelton/Felucca and every fork or firmware built on it (Felucca Salt,
  Felucca 8 Patterns, Hortator, GHOULBOX, Melodee, Skiff, ...);
- zvenson/dinghy and anything built on it;
- the F-Emulator / fm1-emu repository's `fm1-sid/` directory, its
  `probes/lcdtest.c`, and its emulator source (`crates/`);
- any other FM-1 firmware source;
- M-VAVE's stock firmware and any disassembly or function database of it
  (including AL-255/FM-1-RE's `firmware-images/` and disassembly material);
- in this repository: `vendor/emulator/` and `harness/` source (spec side's
  work), and spec-side session transcripts (`sessions/spec/`), which
  contain emulator source. A clean folder never has their contents, not
  even in `.git`: clean sessions run with git's lazy fetching off
  (`GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1`, from `config/claude/clean.json`), so a history
  command that would need them (`git log -p`, `git show`, `git diff`
  across commits) fails instead of downloading them. Give such commands a
  pathspec that leaves the three folders out, and update the folder only
  with `tools/clean-update.sh`. People working in a clean folder by hand
  set `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` in their shell too;
- the sites hugelton.github.io and thefirmwarehub.com;
- the port repository `small-beeps-ports` and a porter's `port-work/`
  folder (the porter's GPL ports; since day-1024).
- FM-1-RE's `docs/io/09-storage.md` (since evening-1024, the owner's
  decision): most of it describes the stock firmware's own code (its
  routines and its own record and patch storage). The spec side may still
  read it and cites only its hardware facts in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, which is
  how those facts reach the firmware side. `tools/check-transcripts.py`
  applies this entry to sessions from 2026-10-25 on (M7 read the document
  while it was allowed; docs/EXPOSURE.md).

`tools/check-transcripts.py` checks every archived clean-side session against
this list (its `FORBIDDEN` table mirrors it; change both together). Since
M4 it fails a call that accesses listed material (reads, lists, searches,
fetches or checks it out) and logs, report only, one that only mentions it
(sessions/README.md).

### Firmware side may use

Log every use in PROVENANCE.md (an ID, the source, what was learned, where it
was used) and name the ID in the commit's `Sources:` field:

- `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, once it exists (each fact there already cites its own
  source);
- JieLi's AC79 SDK, `Jieli-Tech/fw-AC79_AIoT_SDK` (Gitee), Apache-2.0:
  headers, register definitions, drivers. Not its prebuilt libraries;
- AL-255/FM-1-RE (GitHub, WTFPL): its hardware, memory-map, boot-chain and
  update-protocol documents only, except `docs/io/09-storage.md` (see the
  list above). Fetch single documents by URL; never clone it (a clone puts
  its firmware images and disassembly material on disk);
- public datasheets;
- our own experiments: test programs run in the emulator, observed only
  through the harness: `tools/fwtest`, whose manual is docs/HARNESS.md;
- answers to spec requests (docs/SPEC-REQUESTS.md), which arrive as facts
  in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`;
- a porter's reports in `ports/` (measurements and API requests, in
  general terms; CONTRIBUTING.md, "Roles").

### Barriers

- **Clean folder.** `tools/clean-setup.sh [DIR]` creates the clean working
  folder: a blob-less clone with a sparse checkout that leaves out
  `vendor/emulator/`, `harness/` and `sessions/spec/` (and marks them
  `-diff` for history commands), plus the Claude Code settings in
  `config/claude/clean.json`, which deny reading those paths, fetching the
  forbidden sites and cloning the forbidden repositories, and turn git's
  lazy fetching off. `tools/clean-update.sh` updates a clean folder and
  checks nothing excluded arrived; C-CLEAN-FOLDER tests all of this in CI.
- **Records in a clean folder.** Each record on the `records` branch also
  keeps the harness's own test results and the hashes of their outputs.
  Records before SR-1-SR-2 also keep the spec experiments' outputs (memory
  dumps, captures, audio); since then a record keeps only their names and
  SHA-256 (`spec-experiments.sha256`), and older records stay as they are.
  Clean sessions never fetch the records branch wholesale (no `git archive`, checkout or
  lazy fetch of a whole record or of the branch): they fetch only named
  files of the firmware's own records, `report.json`, `report.md` and
  named logs under `logs/`, one path at a time. `tools/clean-update.sh`
  also stops if a file under a `harness/` or `spec-experiments/` folder,
  or under the excluded folders, is in `.git` through any branch, the
  records branch included (since M1, after a wholesale fetch brought 17
  such outputs into a clean folder; docs/EXPOSURE.md).
  `tools/spec-setup.sh [DIR]` does the same for spec side with
  `config/claude/spec.json`.
- **One list of the spec-side folders.** `config/spec-side-folders` names
  the three folders once (since M3). The barrier tools build every name,
  pattern and exclusion from it, and their tests use made-up names
  (`tests/helpers.py`), so changing them needs no command that names the
  folders. Scratch test repositories made by hand use the made-up names
  too. The deny lists keep their literal paths (Claude Code's syntax), and
  C-UNIT checks they cover every folder on the list and that no barrier
  tool or test spells one out.
- **Deny lists only grow.** Never remove or loosen an entry in
  `config/claude/*.json`. Check C-DENY-LISTS fails if one is dropped.
- **Session banner.** Both configs run `tools/session-banner.sh` on every
  SessionStart (startup, resume, clear, compact). It prints the role,
  `claude --version`, the SHA-256 of `.claude/settings.json` and of the
  committed config, and the UTC time, and prints `CONFIG MISMATCH` and exits
  non-zero if they differ.
- **Session transcripts.** Each milestone gets a fresh session. At the start
  of every session, before anything else:
  1. archive the previous session's transcript with
     `python3 tools/archive-session.py <transcript.jsonl> --role <role>`
     (it redacts secrets and private paths, writes the copy to
     `sessions/<role>/` and a note beside it). A spec session may archive
     the previous session of either role; a clean session archives only
     clean sessions and never opens `sessions/spec/` (sessions/README.md);
  2. run `python3 tools/check-transcripts.py`;
  3. add this session's entry to docs/EXPOSURE.md.
  A session never archives its own live transcript; the next one does.

### Spec-side text discipline

What the spec side learns from emulator source leaves `vendor/emulator/`
and `harness/` only through two doors: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` (facts only, each
sourced) and `docs/HARNESS.md` (the harness as a black box). Everything else
the firmware side can read, so spec-side commit messages, pull request
titles and descriptions, and every file outside those two folders and
`sessions/spec/` (docs, tools, tests, records, release notes) describe what
changed in general terms, never emulator internals: no register names,
addresses, struct or function names, or code excerpts. Such detail goes in
comments inside `harness/`. CI logs and records from harness runs show
results (pass/fail, hashes, images, numbers), never emulator source.
`tools/check-emulator-terms.py` (C-SEP-TERMS) looks for identifiers that
occur only in `vendor/emulator/` in all of those places and reports a hit
by place and hash, never the word; run it (with `--show`, in a spec folder)
on your commit messages before you push. People review the two doors, so a
term that occurs in either of them as merged on main is accepted everywhere
(read from main's commit, never the working tree: a term a branch adds to a
door is still a hit until that change has merged). Other reviewed false
positives are listed by hash in `config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json`.
Since M4b the terms of the vendored Plaits (`vendor/plaits/`, read only from
its checksum-verified files) are public like the SDK's, the check says how
many emulator terms that takes off, and `vendor/plaits/` itself is not
scanned, except its `SOURCE.md`, which we write (R-SEP-1).

## Commit messages

Every commit follows `.gitmessage` (run `tools/install-hooks.sh` once to make
it git's template and turn on the commit-msg hook):

```
<area>: <what changed, one line>

What:    what this commit does
Why:     the reason (the milestone and requirement IDs it serves)
How:     the approach, and anything tried and rejected
Result:  what the author saw when testing (the CI record is the authoritative result)
Sources: PROVENANCE IDs used (or "none")
Exposure: the author's role and exposure (e.g. "firmware side, none")
```

- `<area>` is lower-case: `docs`, `tools`, `ci`, `firmware`, `vendor`,
  `config`, `sessions`, and so on.
- A field may continue on following lines, indented.
- Agent-written commits end with the trailers `Model: <exact model ID>` and
  `Claude-Session: <session URL>` (and `Co-Authored-By:`). Their author is
  the agent; the owner is the committer.
- Small commits: one idea each.
- Merge commits are exempt from the template; the pull request they merge
  carries the sections.

`tools/check-commit-msg.py` enforces this in the hook and in CI (C-COMMIT-MSG).

## Pull requests and merging

- Agents and contributors commit **unsigned** on branches and open a pull
  request using `.github/pull_request_template.md` (the same sections, plus
  links to the CI run and the record).
- CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) must pass.
- The **owner merges with GitHub's merge button** ("Create a merge commit").
  GitHub commits and signs the merge commit as `web-flow` (shown as
  Verified) and records the owner as the pull request's `merged_by`. No
  squash or rebase merges, and nobody bypasses the rules.
- Records (`records/<sha>/` on the `records` branch) are written only by
  `.github/workflows/records.yml`, for pushes to main, and the similarity
  audit's report beside it (`records/<sha>/audit/`) only by
  `.github/workflows/audit.yml`'s record job (docs/AUDIT.md). Both use the
  `records` environment's deploy key.
- **Performance budgets** (`config/budgets.json`, R-PERF-1) are raised, or
  moved to the next milestone's, only by a pull request of their own that
  says why in the What/Why/How/Result sections and changes nothing else.
  When CI's performance summary shows an improvement of more than 3%
  (R-PERF-2), say so in the pull request's Result.
- Milestones end with a tag `mN`, signed by the owner with their SSH key
  (below), and a GitHub release with the build outputs, the record and an
  SBOM.

### Merge policy and its history

- **2026-10-21:** the owner first chose to sign every merge with their own
  SSH key, as the ruleset's only bypass actor, because GitHub's button signs
  with GitHub's key instead.
- **2026-10-22:** pull request #1 was merged with the button. Its merge
  commit `2fd28219` is signed by GitHub (`web-flow`, verified), and its
  record shows C-MERGE **FAIL** under the old rule ("committer is web-flow,
  not the owner"). The record stays as it is, and history is not rewritten.
- **2026-10-22:** the owner then chose button merges for good. The bypass
  was removed from the main ruleset, so the rules now apply to everyone.

What a merge on main proves: GitHub's signature shows the commit was made
by GitHub on the owner's merge. `merged_by` shows the owner pressed the
button. The required `ci` check shows CI passed on exactly the merged head.
The records workflow re-checks all of this for every push to main
(C-MERGE): a merge commit, a verified signature, committer `web-flow` with
the pull request's `merged_by` the owner (or, for older merges, the owner
as committer), and its second parent the head of a pull request whose `ci`
run passed. Otherwise the record says **FAIL** for C-MERGE, and the record
is still written.

## Rulesets

Repository rulesets (Settings → Rules → Rulesets):

- **main**: restrict deletions; block force pushes; require a pull request
  before merging (allowed merge method: merge only); require status checks to
  pass (the `ci` job); no bypass (until 2026-10-22: the repository admin
  role).
- **records-history** (branch `records`): restrict deletions; block force
  pushes; no bypass.
- **records-writer** (branch `records`): restrict creations; restrict
  updates; bypass list: deploy keys only. Together these make the records
  workflow's deploy key the only writer, and it can only add commits.
- **milestone-tags** (tags `m*`): restrict deletions; restrict updates; no
  bypass.

Repository settings: allow merge commits only (squash and rebase merging
off).

Set up on 2026-10-22 by session M0a, with the owner's approval, through the
GitHub API:

|------|-------------------|
| Ruleset `main` | 25612787 (required check `ci` from GitHub Actions; no bypass since 2026-10-22, before that the repository admin role) |
| Ruleset `records-history` | 25612788 |

## SSH signing for milestone tags (one-time setup, owner)

1. Create a signing key (or reuse an SSH key you already have):
   `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "small-beeps signing" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing`
2. Tell git to sign with it:
   ```sh
   git config --global gpg.format ssh
   git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing.pub
   git config --global tag.gpgSign true
   ```
   Leave `commit.gpgSign` off: merges are signed by GitHub's button.
3. Let git verify signatures locally: add a line
   `<your git email> <contents of id_ed25519_signing.pub>` to
   `~/.ssh/allowed_signers`, then
   `git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile ~/.ssh/allowed_signers`.
4. On GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → Key type
   **Signing Key**, and paste the `.pub` contents.
5. Tag a milestone: `git tag -s mN -m "mN"`, then `git push origin mN`.
6. Check: `git tag -v mN` shows "Good "git" signature", and GitHub shows the
   tag as **Verified**.

## Licences

- Every file we write starts with an SPDX header:
  `SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT` and `SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98`.
  Files that can't carry one are covered in `REUSE.toml`.
- Vendored files keep their own licences (`vendor/*/LICENSE`, `NOTICE`).
- CI runs `reuse lint` and fails on any gap (C-REUSE).
- Never commit the toolchain or anything containing it (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md).
- Nothing secret ever goes in: no keys, tokens or private notes. The
  repository is public and history is never rewritten.

## Privacy

The repository is public. No committed file, commit message or pull request
text names the owner's username, real name, e-mail address, hostname or
local folder names, or a full local path: write paths relative to the
repository, or as `~/...` with the top folder shown as `<top>`. Anyone who
finds such a term in the repository tells the owner instead of repeating it.

- **The terms** are kept by the owner, never in the repository: in the
  gitignored `tools/[REDACTED:host]` (one per line, `#` comments,
  matched ignoring case) and in the repository secret `PRIVATE_TERMS`, which
  CI passes to the check.
- **The check** `tools/check-private.py` (C-PRIVATE, R-PUB-3) scans every
  tracked file and every commit message, and the pre-commit and commit-msg
  hooks scan staged files and the message (`tools/install-hooks.sh` turns
  them on). A hit is reported by file and line only, never the term. CI
  fails when the secret is missing.
- **Records are scanned too** (since M1). Before a test record, an audit
  report or a C-MERGE re-check is hashed, uploaded or pushed, any file in
  it holding a term is withheld: deleted, and listed with the SHA-256 of
  the original in `WITHHELD.json`, which the record keeps (C-RECORD-PRIVATE).
  The original is not kept anywhere; the checks are deterministic, so it
  can be regenerated and matched to its hash. CI artifacts are kept 14 days.
- **Older records stay as they are.** A file under `sessions/` or
  `docs/prompts/` whose blob is identical to the same path at the base
  commit in `config/private-base` (the last main commit before the check)
  is exempt. This is decided from git's object hashes alone, so no session
  opens or lists the spec side's transcripts for it, and the check prints
  only how many files it exempted per folder. Every file added or changed
  after the base is checked in full. Files that sessions keep editing get no
  exemption: their current text is redacted instead (`docs/EXPOSURE.md` was,
  on 2026-10-22), and git history keeps the originals.
- **Archived transcripts** are redacted by `tools/archive-session.py`: the
  username anywhere it appears, the local top-level folder as `<top>`, and
  every private term.

## Low profile (for now)

The repository is public but unpromoted. In its name, description and topics,
and in README.md, never use these quiet words: **FM-1, M-VAVE, JieLi, synth,
firmware** (any spelling or case; `tools/check-low-profile.py` has the
patterns). Don't link the repository from anywhere, star it, fork it or
announce it. Everything else in the repository stays complete and truthful.
docs/GOING-PUBLIC.md says how this ends.

#!/bin/sh
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Updates a clean folder to its remote's main (or REF), the safe way.
#
#   tools/clean-update.sh [--dir DIR] [REF]      (default: this folder, main)
#
# Clean sessions run with git's lazy fetching off (GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1, set
# by config/claude/clean.json), so no command can download a file the clean
# folder leaves out. A checkout of new commits needs lazy fetching for the
# files it does check out, so this script allows it for exactly one
# fast-forward, then re-applies the sparse checkout and checks that no file
# under a spec-side folder (config/spec-side-folders) reached the disk or the
# folder's .git, nor any spec-side file under another branch (the records
# branch keeps spec-side outputs). Stop and tell the owner if it fails.
#
# The fast-forward runs with --no-stat and -q: a merge summary (diffstat)
# counts the lines of every changed file, and with lazy fetching allowed git
# downloads the excluded files' contents to count them.
set -eu

ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
if [ "${1:-}" = "--dir" ]; then ROOT=$(cd "$2" && pwd); shift 2; fi
ref=${1:-main}
role=$(cat "$ROOT/.claude/small-beeps-role" 2>/dev/null || true)
[ "$role" = clean ] || { echo "clean-update.sh is for clean folders (role here: ${role:-none})" >&2; exit 2; }

GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" fetch -q origin
env -u GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH git -C "$ROOT" merge -q --no-stat --ff-only "origin/$ref"
GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 sh "$ROOT/tools/clean-setup.sh" > /dev/null

# The spec-side folders, from the one list (since M3).
SPEC_FOLDERS=$(grep -v '^#' "$ROOT/config/spec-side-folders" | cut -f1)
[ -n "$SPEC_FOLDERS" ] || { echo "STOP: no spec-side folders in config/spec-side-folders"; exit 1; }
# Any path with one of them, or a spec-experiments/ folder, in it.
SPEC_RE="(^|/)(spec-experiments|$(printf '%s\n' "$SPEC_FOLDERS" | paste -sd '|' -))/"
fail=0
for p in $SPEC_FOLDERS; do
    [ ! -e "$ROOT/$p" ] || { echo "STOP: $p is on disk"; fail=1; }
    have=$(GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" ls-tree -r HEAD -- "$p" | awk '$2 == "blob" { print $3 }' \
        | GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" cat-file --batch-check='%(objectname)' 2>/dev/null | grep -vc missing || true)
    [ "$have" = 0 ] || { echo "STOP: $have file(s) under $p are in .git"; fail=1; }
done
# Spec-side outputs can reach .git another way: each record on the records
# branch keeps fwtest's own and the spec experiments' outputs, and fetching
# a record's files wholesale brings their blobs in (it happened once, in
# M1; docs/EXPOSURE.md). So under every branch, remote branch included, a
# file under a folder named spec-experiments/ or as a spec-side folder, at
# any depth, must be missing too.
# Trees are in a blob-less clone, so this reads no file.
have=$(GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" for-each-ref --format='%(objectname)' refs/heads refs/remotes \
    | sort -u | while read -r c; do GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" ls-tree -r "$c"; done \
    | awk -F '\t' -v re="$SPEC_RE" '{ split($1, m, " ") } m[2] == "blob" && $2 ~ re { print m[3] }' \
    | sort -u | GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 git -C "$ROOT" cat-file --batch-check='%(objectname)' 2>/dev/null | grep -vc missing || true)
[ "$have" = 0 ] || { echo "STOP: $have spec-side output or source file(s) reached through a branch (the records branch?) are in .git"; fail=1; }
if [ $fail -ne 0 ]; then echo "Tell the owner before doing anything else." >&2; exit 1; fi
echo "clean folder at $(git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse --short HEAD); no spec-side files on disk or in .git"

# Session transcripts

Every agent session that works on this repository is kept here as evidence.
A session's transcript is the full record of what it read, searched,
fetched, ran and wrote, so anyone can check that a firmware-side (clean)
session never touched forbidden material (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Clean-room
rules"; R-CLEAN-1, R-CLEAN-3).

## Folders, and who archives whom

- `clean/`: firmware-side (clean) sessions.
- `spec/`: spec-side sessions. Their transcripts contain emulator source,

  clean settings deny reading it.

A **spec** session may archive the previous session of either role. A
**clean** session archives only clean sessions, and never opens, lists or
searches anything under `spec/`. When the previous session was spec side
and the next is clean, the clean session leaves it for the next spec
session to archive.

An **auditor** session (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Roles") is never archived here:
its transcript holds GPL source, so it goes to the owner's private
repository, and docs/EXPOSURE.md records its ID, SHA-256 and that
repository's commit. `tools/check-transcripts.py` fails on any transcript
outside `clean/` and `spec/`.

Each role folder holds:

- `<date>-<role>-<id>.jsonl`: the session's Claude Code transcript, one JSON
  entry per line, as Claude Code wrote it under `~/.claude/projects/`, with
  secrets and private details redacted. `<date>` is the UTC date of its first
  entry, `<role>` is `clean` or `spec`, and `<id>` is the Claude Code session
  ID.
- `<same name>.REDACTIONS.md`: what was redacted (kind and count), with the
  SHA-256 of the original and of the redacted copy. The owner keeps the
  originals, so a redacted copy can be matched to its original if that is
  ever challenged.
- `<same name>.subagents/`: transcripts of subagents the session started, if

A session never archives itself, because its transcript is still being

# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT

ghcr.io/japes98/small-beeps@sha256:8402225f79ae01306cab6a25b2776369c52fd1ffc1c71eb1556a94c0c2b8a116
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""tools/fwtest runs an image pinned by digest (R-SEP-3, R-HARN-10; check
C-FWTEST-PIN).

  check-fwtest-pin.py

config/fwtest-image must hold one image reference of the form
`ghcr.io/<owner>/<repository>@sha256:<64 hex digits>`, with no quiet words
in it (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Low profile"), or `unpublished` until the first
image is published (tools/fwtest then refuses to run). tools/fwtest must
take the image from that file, check for the digest form, and run it with
no network, as linux/amd64, with the working folder mounted read-only.
"""
import os
import re

config: pin fwtest 0.6.0; fmgold ends 1 ms clear of a block

What:    config/fwtest-image moves to fwtest 0.6.0's digest (sha256:8402225f…a116,
         as #112). fmgold and fmgold2 run to 4199 ms (was 4200), and their
         golden WAV is the old one less its last 64-frame block.
Why:     on 0.6.0 fmgold's WAV came out 128 samples (one block) short. Not
         start-up: the first flash write is the selection's settled save at
         2000.6 ms (4 KiB erase, two page programs, 18 ms busy). Core 0 polls
         the status register meanwhile, 48 848 more instructions, so the
         run's late end (docs/HARNESS.md, "Time") lands at another
         instruction phase: 4200.243 ms on 0.6.0 against 4200.406 on 0.5.0,
         and block 2894 ends at 4200.406. The audio is the same sample for
         sample over the common length. At 4200 the end sat within 2 us of a
         block's end, so any change in core 0's instruction count could move
         it; re-recording at 4200 would pass until the next such change.
How:     --ms 4199 ends at 4199.24 to 4199.33 ms, about 1.1 ms before the
         next block ends; the golden is fwtest's own output.
Result:  fmgold at 4199 ms gives the same bytes on 0.5.0 and 0.6.0, a strict
         prefix of the old golden (the block dropped is silent). Full
         firmware suite on 0.6.0: PASS.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""The timing goldens' policy (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, "Timing goldens"),
for the suites that compare fwtest's outputs with golden files.

A bigger or slower image starts a few microseconds later, and every
event of the firmware's that waits on an audio block can then move by a
block (1.451 ms) or by a MIDI byte (0.320 ms). The rules:

1. A run's end clears the audio blocks: the end asked for (--ms) falls
   at least END_BEFORE_MS before the next block's end and at least
   END_AFTER_MS after the last one. An end comes late, never early, while
   core 0 waits (docs/HARNESS.md, "Time"), and start-up only moves the
   blocks later, so the margins say how far either can go before the run
   takes one block more or less (check_end, from the run's ipb.csv).
2. MIDI out's captures are compared with a stated tolerance: the same
   bytes in the same order (the same messages, decoded), each at its
   golden time within MIDI_TOL_MS: a block and two bytes (compare_midi).
   Screens that show the live spectrum while a sound plays are compared
   exactly outside its rectangle (LIVE), which shows the sound's last
   few blocks and so moves with them; the spectrum case checks the bars
   themselves through the interface's record (compare_screen).
3. Goldens are written again only by tools/regolden.py, which proves the
   change a pure time shift first (the same bytes, notes and sound) and
   writes nothing otherwise (the shift_* functions here).
"""

import hashlib
import json
import os
import struct
import wave
import zlib

BLOCK_FRAMES = 64                       # stereo frames a block (firmware/src/audio.h)
BLOCK_MS = BLOCK_FRAMES * 544 / 24000.0  # 1.451 ms (HW-45)
BYTE_MS = 0.32                          # a MIDI byte on the wire
END_BEFORE_MS = 1.0
END_AFTER_MS = 0.2
MIDI_TOL_MS = BLOCK_MS + 2 * BYTE_MS    # 2.091 ms
QUIET = 1                               # |sample| at or under this is quiet: a level held at -96 dB leaves +-1
GAP_FRAMES = 2 * BLOCK_FRAMES           # quiet frames that part two sounds
MAX_SHIFT_FRAMES = 16 * BLOCK_FRAMES    # how far one sound may move (23 ms)
# The live spectrum on the patch view (firmware/src/views.c: SPEC_X,
# SPEC_Y, SPEC_BARS bars 4 pixels apart, SPEC_H): x, y, width, height.
LIVE = [(8, 150, 56 * 4, 40)]


# --- 1. A run's end -------------------------------------------------------

### 2026-10-26 overnight-1025: timing goldens

The owner's answer to ARP's question 6 ("timing goldens keep moving"):
a policy, built in `tools/goldtime.py` and `tools/regolden.py`, and
applied to the firmware suite's and the arpeggiator's cases
(R-GOLD-1 to R-GOLD-3).

- **Why they moved.** A bigger image starts a few microseconds later
  (start-up clears more RAM before the time base starts, about 2 us a
  KiB), and anything of ours that waits for an audio block (1.451 ms)
  then sometimes waits one more: a MIDI byte taken a block later, a
  note a block later, a MIDI out byte queued behind another (320 us).
  And a run's end comes late while core 0 waits (docs/HARNESS.md,
  "Time"), by an amount that moves with core 0's instructions, so a run
  that ended near a block's end sometimes took that block and sometimes
  didn't: a WAV a block longer or shorter. fmgold at `--ms 4200` ended
  2 us from one.
- **1. A run's end clears the blocks.** Every case that keeps its
  blocks' times (`--ipb`) and is compared with a golden ends at least
  `END_BEFORE_MS` (1 ms) before the next block's end, so a late end
  takes no extra block, and `END_AFTER_MS` (0.2 ms, about 100 KiB of
  start-up) after the last, so start-up moving the blocks later loses
  none. A block is 1.451 ms, so the window is 0.25 ms wide; "1 ms clear"
  on both sides cannot be had. `check_end` works it out from the run's
  own `ipb.csv` and suggests the nearest tenth of a millisecond that
  keeps it; tools/fw-suite.py and tools/arp_suite.py fail a case that
  doesn't; the ends are put in the middle of their window (about 0.1 ms
  of room each way) and in the same block as before where they can be,
  so the runs take the blocks they took. 30 of the suite's cases and 24
  of the arpeggiator's moved, each by about a millisecond or less (the
  arpeggiator's in its `END_MS`: each run starts from its own
  flash chip, so its blocks fall at their own times). The store's cases are left as they are: their goldens are
  screens taken mid-run, which no end moves, and only one keeps
  `ipb.csv` (a load test with no golden).
- **2. MIDI out's captures, with a tolerance.** fwtest compares golden
  files byte for byte, and `rel-percent` would let a byte written as
  hex digits differ too, so midiout's, midithru's, midilocal's and
  midiburst's captures moved to `tests/fw/golden-midi/`, which
  tools/fw-suite.py compares itself: the same bytes in the same order
  (and the same messages, decoded), each within `MIDI_TOL_MS`, 2.091
  ms (a block and two bytes), of its golden time. The arpeggiator's
  goldens were already without times.
- **3. Written again only when proven a time shift.**
  `tools/regolden.py --out <the suite's --out>` compares each golden
  with the run's output of the same name and prints `same`, `shift` or
  `REFUSED`; `--write` writes the shifts, and nothing at all if any is
  refused. A shift is proven:
  - for MIDI captures, by the same bytes (or messages) in the same
    order, only their times moved;
  - for a WAV, by the same sounds (runs of frames over +-1, parted by
    128 quiet frames), in the same order, each sample for sample the
    golden's, each moved by a whole number of frames (at most 1 024);
    a sound cut by either run's end need only match as far as both go;
  - for the arpeggiator's sound hashes (`--arp-out`, `--arp-old`, the
    suite's outputs on the new and on the base image), by the base
    run's WAV giving the golden hash and the two WAVs being a shift;
  - for anything else (screens, consoles, RAM captures), only by being
    identical.
  A golden whose content changes is a change of behaviour: made in the
  commit that changes the behaviour, which says so.
  `tools/arp_suite.py --write-golden` now writes only goldens a run
  doesn't have yet; `--replace` overwrites one that differs (a change
  of behaviour).
- **Live screens.** The patch view's live spectrum (views.c, `SPEC_X`,
  `SPEC_Y`, 56 bars of 4 pixels, `SPEC_H`) shows the last few blocks of
  sound, so a shift moves its bars: macros', midipanel's and spectrum's
  screens moved to `tests/fw/golden-live/`, compared exactly outside that
  rectangle (`compare_screen`); the spectrum case checks the bars through
  the interface's record.
- **The arpeggiator's inputs, off its grid.** Its runs let their keys go
  exactly on a step (2 000 ms is 96 clock pulses, and every rate's hold a
  whole number of steps), and one by one, 30 ms apart, so a step could
  fall among them; the stuck run had panel events on 1/16 steps and two
  keys pressed at the same instant. Which came first moved with a few
  microseconds. The keys now go together, 10 ms (`OFF_GRID_MS`) after
  the grid; stuck's later events 7 ms off it, its two keys 10 ms apart;
  its golden messages were written again for that (a change of its
  input), and it keeps no sound hash (its last notes are panel keys
  whose starts and ends come by the key scan and the block, so their
  lengths move by a scan).
- **Proven on real outputs.** The clock-out change (this session) moved
  the four MIDI captures by 1 us: `regolden` called each a shift; under
  the tolerance they pass as they are. A test build, `SB_TEST_LATE_START`
  (firmware/src/main.c), starts late, as a bigger image would:
  - **About 0.4 ms late** (twice the 0.2 ms margin): every end check
    fires, and `regolden` refused what is not a shift: fmgold (a note 98
    frames longer: its start and end came by different paths), midiout
    (the same messages, but two more status bytes: running status
    follows the gaps between messages), the live screens (before they
    were masked), and the arpeggiator's runs whose inputs sat on its
    grid. That is the size of shift the policy does not absorb.
  - **About 0.14 ms late** (the build as committed): every golden of the
    firmware suite passes as it is (the MIDI captures moved by up to 1.3
    ms, within the tolerance; the live screens the same outside the
    spectrum; fmgold identical), and `regolden` proves all eight changed
    files shifts. The arpeggiator's runs all pass. Only the end check
    fires (0.18 to 0.2 ms after a block, under its 0.2): the early
    warning, answered by moving `--ms` within its block, which changes no
    golden.

I finished all four parts in four PRs to main, plus the six candidates on draft #126. CI passes on all five. No release was made.

## Questions for the owner
1. **Steam Pipes (P68) breath:** your recipe said "a low-level, feedback-heavy modulator". In this engine a quiet feedback operator makes no noise at all. So the breath is a full-level feedback modulator driving a quiet second carrier, about 25 dB under the pipe. Is that acceptable?
2. **Tutti Swell's stab sits 15 dB under the swell.** The pads rule needs a pad to take at least 50 ms to get within 3 dB of its peak, which caps the stab. For a louder stab I'd move it to "brass and winds"; should I?
3. **How I read "1 ms clear of block boundaries":** a run ends at least 1 ms before the next block's end and at least 0.2 ms after the last one. A block is only 1.451 ms, so 1 ms on both sides is impossible. When code shifts the blocks, the check fails CI and names a new `--ms` within the same block, which changes no golden. That already happened once on #126 (six ARP runs). Should it fail CI, or only warn?
4. **Exceptions to "goldens re-recorded only by the tool":**
   - Five screens showing the live spectrum are now compared exactly except inside the spectrum's rectangle.
   - The stuck run no longer has a sound hash.
   - Some test inputs changed on purpose, and their goldens were rewritten by hand and labelled as such: the ARP runs' key releases moved off the step grid, stuck's events and key presses were moved apart, and env's 1400 ms screen moved to 1600 ms.

   Are these acceptable?
5. **Clock out after a clean Stop:** ours resumes 250 ms after the sender's last clock. A downstream follower therefore sees a 250 ms gap even when the sender simply stopped. Is that OK?
6. **Release details:**
   - Pushing a tag that isn't listed in `config/releases.json` (m2–m8) makes the workflow fail. Should m2–m8 get versions?
   - `record.tree_sha256` is the hash of the record's `SHA256SUMS`, which a clean folder isn't allowed to fetch. Should it be added to the allowed list? Until then it's typed in by hand locally.
   - `build.container` holds the build image's local ID; a locally built image has no registry digest.
7. **Still open from ARP:** the stack (576 of 768 bytes; SEQ will likely need a raise), and the one compiler crash, which hasn't recurred.

## What was done
- **#135, session start:** ARP's transcript archived, with six REVIEWED.json entries for its two worktree sparse-checkout calls (listed in the PR). The prompt is saved, and your answers to ARP's questions are in PLAN.md's open items.
- **#138, timing goldens policy:**
  - `tools/goldtime.py` checks run ends from each run's own block times. The ends were moved to the middle of their allowed window.
  - MIDI captures moved to `tests/fw/golden-midi/` and are compared with a 2.091 ms tolerance.
  - `tools/regolden.py` rewrites a golden only after proving the change is a pure time shift, and writes nothing if any file fails.
  - **Late-start test:** I built an image that starts ~0.14 ms late. Every golden passed as it was, and `regolden` proved all 8 changed files were pure shifts. At 0.4 ms late it correctly refused the files that weren't pure shifts.
- **#139, clock out:** our clock out stays quiet while any clock comes in, with a new test case (`clock-quiet`, MIDI thru on). The test fails on main's image and passes on the new one. No golden needed rewriting: the MIDI captures moved by 1 µs, inside the tolerance.
- **#140, M9 app release:**
  - It follows the spec side's format 1.0 in #136. My own first draft of the format was replaced when #136 appeared.
  - `tools/release.py` / `release.sh` build the release; `tools/fm1img.py` is the reference reader, running the app's seven checks in order.
  - The workflow only makes draft releases, never creates a tag, and never replaces a file. `m9` is set to 0.9.0, and C-RELEASE tests that a release built twice is identical.
  - `docs/RELEASING.md` covers cutting, checking and loading a release.
  - A local dry run on tag m1 (nothing published) rebuilt m1's image byte for byte.
- **#126 (still a draft):**
  - **Candidates P65–P70:** Tutti Swell, Round Seq, Neon Riff, Steam Pipes, Hammer Keys and Wire Bass, with my own numbers. Each was measured against its recipe with a new `tools/preset_measure.py`, and the figures are in DESIGN-NOTES. No voice bank was opened and no factory names are used.
  - **Results:** all 70 presets pass, and the 64 existing hashes are unchanged.
  - **Merge:** tonight's chain is merged in.
- **Listening:** `~/Development/<top>/drop/presets/` has `65-…wav` to `70-…wav`, and INDEX.md is updated.

One gap in the register: EXPOSURE.md says I saw only #137's title, but late on I also printed its changed-file list (names only). The next session's entry can add that line.

**Merge order:** #136 → #135 → #138 → #139 → #140 → #134 → #137. #134 and #137 need main merged in first, keeping both EXPOSURE.md entries. #126 stays a draft and is not for merging.

# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# The app release of a signed milestone tag (docs/RELEASING.md; R-REL-1 to
# R-REL-3). Builds it with tools/release.sh (main's tools; the tag's own
# files and build script) and attaches it to the tag's GitHub release, a
# draft made here if the release doesn't exist yet. It never makes a tag
# (`gh release create --verify-tag` refuses a missing one), refuses a tag
# GitHub doesn't show as Verified or that config/releases.json gives no
# version, and never replaces a file a release already has.
name: release

on:
  push:
    tags: ["m*"]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: "The signed tag to release (config/releases.json must list it)"
        required: true
      publish:
        description: "Attach the files to the release (otherwise only the workflow's artifact)"
        type: boolean
        default: false

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 30
    outputs:
      tag: ${{ steps.tag.outputs.tag }}
    steps:
      # main's tools, whatever the tag (older tags have no release tools).
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          ref: main
          fetch-depth: 0
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-python@6d4fd22b20465ccc0f7354476588e8df7c9ca0e0 # v7.1.0
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: The tag
        id: tag
        env:
          TAG: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref_name || inputs.tag }}
        run: |
          set -eu
          case "$TAG" in m[0-9]*) ;; *) echo "::error::not a milestone tag: $TAG"; exit 1 ;; esac
          git fetch --no-tags origin "+refs/tags/$TAG:refs/tags/$TAG"
          echo "tag=$TAG" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: The records branch
        run: git fetch --no-tags origin +refs/heads/records:refs/remotes/origin/records

      - name: Build the release (tools/release.sh)
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          TAG: ${{ steps.tag.outputs.tag }}
        run: sh tools/release.sh "$TAG" --out out/release --records-ref origin/records

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2
        with:
          name: release-${{ steps.tag.outputs.tag }}
          path: out/release
          if-no-files-found: error

  publish:
    needs: build
    if: github.event_name == 'push' || inputs.publish
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 10
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@37930b1c2abaa49bbe596cd826c3c89aef350131 # v7.0.0
        with:
          name: release-${{ needs.build.outputs.tag }}
          path: release

      - name: Attach to the tag's release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          TAG: ${{ needs.build.outputs.tag }}
        run: |
          set -eu
          version=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("release/release.json"))["version"])')
          if ! gh release view "$TAG" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            {
              echo "The app release $version of \`$TAG\`, for the F-Emulator app (docs/RELEASING.md)."
              echo
              echo "Built by the release workflow from the signed tag's commit and checked against its test record;"
              echo "\`release.json\` names the commit, the record's tree hash and the fwtest it passed on;"
              echo "the app opens \`small-beeps-$version.fm1img\` (docs/M9-PLAN.md, \"The release format\")."
              echo
              echo '```'
              cat release/SHA256SUMS
              echo '```'
            } > notes.md
            gh release create "$TAG" --verify-tag --draft --title "$TAG: small-beeps $version" --notes-file notes.md
          fi
          have=$(gh release view "$TAG" --json assets --jq '.assets[].name')
          for f in release/*; do
            if printf '%s\n' "$have" | grep -qxF "$(basename "$f")"; then
              echo "::error::$TAG's release already has $(basename "$f"); not replaced"
              exit 1
            fi
          done
          gh release upload "$TAG" release/*
{
  "comment": "App releases (docs/RELEASING.md): each signed milestone tag that gets one, and its version. tools/release.sh and .github/workflows/release.yml refuse a tag not listed. App releases start at 0.9.0 (docs/M9-PLAN.md, the owner's answer 6). Added only by pull request.",
  "versions": {
    "m9": "0.9.0"
  }
}

content.content:
#!/bin/sh
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Makes the app release of a signed milestone tag (docs/RELEASING.md;
# R-REL-1 to R-REL-3), the way .github/workflows/release.yml does:
#
#   tools/release.sh TAG --out DIR [--version X.Y.Z]
#                    [--records-ref REF | --report FILE --record-sums-sha256 HEX]
#
# 1. TAG must be an annotated tag that GitHub shows as Verified (signed by
#    a key of its tagger's account; the GitHub API, through gh). It never
#    makes a tag.
# 2. The version comes from config/releases.json (this folder's), unless
#    --version is given (a dry run for a tag that has none yet).
# 3. The tag's commit's test record: records/<commit>/report.json on REF
#    (by default origin/records), and the SHA-256 of that record's
#    SHA256SUMS (release.json's record.tree_sha256, docs/M9-PLAN.md); or,
#    in a clean folder (which never fetches the records branch, and of a
#    record fetches only report.json, report.md and logs), the report
#    fetched by name and that hash given (a milestone's release notes
#    state it).
# 4. The tag's files, exported as tools/reproduce does (never the
#    spec-side folders), built twice by their own tools/build.sh at two
#    source paths: the same bytes both times, and the record's.
# 5. fwtest's version: the record's fwtest image, asked (tools/fwtest).
# 6. tools/release.py build, twice: the same bytes; then verify.
set -eu

ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
PY=$(sh "$ROOT/tools/find-python.sh")
tag="" out="" version="" ref=origin/records report="" sums=""
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
    case "$1" in
        --out) out=$2; shift 2 ;;
        --version) version=$2; shift 2 ;;
        --records-ref) ref=$2; shift 2 ;;
        --report) report=$2; shift 2 ;;
        --record-sums-sha256) sums=$2; shift 2 ;;
        -*) echo "unknown option $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
        *) tag=$1; shift ;;
    esac
done
[ -n "$tag" ] && [ -n "$out" ] || { echo "usage: $0 TAG --out DIR [...]" >&2; exit 2; }
fail() { echo "release: $*" >&2; exit 1; }

# 1. A signed tag, verified by GitHub.
[ "$(git -C "$ROOT" cat-file -t "refs/tags/$tag" 2>/dev/null)" = tag ] || fail "$tag is not an annotated tag here"
commit=$(git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse --verify "refs/tags/$tag^{commit}")
repo=${GITHUB_REPOSITORY:-$(gh repo view --json nameWithOwner --jq .nameWithOwner)}
tag_sha=$(gh api "repos/$repo/git/ref/tags/$tag" --jq '.object.sha')
[ "$tag_sha" = "$(git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse "refs/tags/$tag")" ] || fail "$tag here is not GitHub's $tag"
verified=$(gh api "repos/$repo/git/tags/$tag_sha" --jq '.verification.verified')
[ "$verified" = true ] || fail "$tag is not signed and verified on GitHub ($(gh api "repos/$repo/git/tags/$tag_sha" --jq '.verification.reason'))"
echo "tag:     $tag ($tag_sha), verified; commit $commit"

# 2. Its version.
if [ -z "$version" ]; then
    version=$("$PY" -I -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))["versions"].get(sys.argv[2], ""))' \
        "$ROOT/config/releases.json" "$tag")
    [ -n "$version" ] || fail "config/releases.json gives $tag no version"
fi
echo "version: $version"

work=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT

# 3. The record.
if [ -z "$report" ]; then
    git -C "$ROOT" show "$ref:records/$commit/report.json" > "$work/report.json" \
        || fail "no record of $commit on $ref"
    git -C "$ROOT" show "$ref:records/$commit/SHA256SUMS" > "$work/record.sums" \
        || fail "the record of $commit on $ref has no SHA256SUMS"
    sums=$("$PY" -I -c 'import hashlib,sys; print(hashlib.sha256(open(sys.argv[1],"rb").read()).hexdigest())' \
        "$work/record.sums")
    report=$work/report.json
fi
[ -n "$sums" ] || fail "--report needs --record-sums-sha256"
echo "record:  records/$commit/, its SHA256SUMS $sums"

# 4. The tag's files, built twice.
sh "$ROOT/tools/reproduce" --export-only "$commit" "$work/src"
sh "$work/src/tools/build.sh" build --out "$work/b1"
sh "$work/src/tools/build.sh" build --out "$work/b2" --src-mount /tmp/elsewhere/small-beeps-src-b
cmp "$work/b1/app.bin" "$work/b2/app.bin" || fail "the two builds differ"

# 5. fwtest's version, of the image the record names.
fwimage=$("$PY" -I -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))["environment"]["fwtest_image"])' "$report")
fwver=$(FWTEST_IMAGE=$fwimage sh "$ROOT/tools/fwtest" version)
echo "fwtest:  $fwver ($fwimage)"

# 6. The release, twice.
created=$(TZ=UTC git -C "$ROOT" log -1 --date=format-local:%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ --format=%cd "$commit")
for d in r1 r2; do
    "$PY" -I "$ROOT/tools/release.py" build --tag "$tag" --version "$version" --commit "$commit" \
        --src "$work/src" --build "$work/b1" --report "$report" --record-sums-sha256 "$sums" \
        --fwtest-version "$fwver" --created "$created" --out "$work/$d"
done
diff -r "$work/r1" "$work/r2" >/dev/null || fail "the two releases differ"
"$PY" -I "$ROOT/tools/release.py" verify "$work/r1"
"$PY" -I "$ROOT/tools/fm1img.py" "$work/r1/small-beeps-$version.fm1img"
mkdir -p "$out"
cp "$work/r1/"* "$out/"
echo "release: $out"
cat "$out/SHA256SUMS"

#    fetched by name and that hash given (a milestone's release notes
#    state it).

#    spec-side folders), built twice by their own tools/build.sh at two
#    source paths: the same bytes both times, and the record's.
# 5. fwtest's version: the record's fwtest image, asked (tools/fwtest).
# 6. tools/release.py build, twice: the same bytes; then verify.

PY=$(sh "$ROOT/tools/find-python.sh")

        --version) version=$2; shift 2 ;;
        --records-ref) ref=$2; shift 2 ;;
        --report) report=$2; shift 2 ;;
        --record-sums-sha256) sums=$2; shift 2 ;;

[ "$(git -C "$ROOT" cat-file -t "refs/tags/$tag" 2>/dev/null)" = tag ] || fail "$tag is not an annotated tag here"
commit=$(git -C "$ROOT" rev-parse --verify "refs/tags/$tag^{commit}")
repo=${GITHUB_REPOSITORY:-$(gh repo view --json nameWithOwner --jq .nameWithOwner)}

[ "$verified" = true ] || fail "$tag is not signed and verified on GitHub ($(gh api "repos/$repo/git/tags/$tag_sha" --jq '.verification.reason'))"
echo "tag:     $tag ($tag_sha), verified; commit $commit"

        "$ROOT/config/releases.json" "$tag")

trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT

if [ -z "$report" ]; then

        || fail "no record of $commit on $ref"
    git -C "$ROOT" show "$ref:records/$commit/SHA256SUMS" > "$work/record.sums" \
        || fail "the record of $commit on $ref has no SHA256SUMS"
    sums=$("$PY" -I -c 'import hashlib,sys; print(hashlib.sha256(open(sys.argv[1],"rb").read()).hexdigest())' \

sh "$ROOT/tools/reproduce" --export-only "$commit" "$work/src"

    else shasum -a 256 "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1; fi
}

image_tag() {
    echo "small-beeps-build:$(sha256 "$ROOT/tools/Dockerfile" | cut -c1-16)"
}

cmd_image() {
    # No build context: the Dockerfile fetches everything it needs.
    docker build --platform "$PLATFORM" -t "$(image_tag)" - < "$ROOT/tools/Dockerfile"
    docker image inspect --format 'image {{.Id}}' "$(image_tag)"
}

cmd_build() {
    out="" src_mount=/mnt/small-beeps-src defines="" demo=""
    while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
        case "$1" in
            --out) out=$2; shift 2 ;;
            --src-mount) src_mount=$2; shift 2 ;;
            --define)
                case "$2" in
                    ''|*[!A-Z0-9_]*) echo "build: --define takes a NAME of A-Z, 0-9 and _" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                defines="$defines $2"; shift 2 ;;
            --demo)
                case "$2" in
                    plaits) demo=$2 ;;
                    *) echo "build: --demo takes plaits" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                shift 2 ;;
            *) echo "unknown option $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    [ -n "$out" ] || { echo "build: --out DIR is required" >&2; exit 2; }
    tag=$(image_tag)
    docker image inspect "$tag" >/dev/null 2>&1 || cmd_image
    rm -rf "$out"
    mkdir -p "$out"
    out=$(cd "$out" && pwd)
    docker run --rm --platform "$PLATFORM" --network none \
        --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e SB_DEFINES="$defines" -e SB_DEMO="$demo" \
        -v "$ROOT:$src_mount:ro" -v "$out:/out" -w "$src_mount" \
        "$tag" sh "$src_mount/tools/build.sh" inside "$src_mount" /out
    cat "$out/SHA256SUMS"

# code (code and constants, in the image, wherever they run), data

# beacon included), image (the raw image's length), stack (reserved at the

# stack) and, since M7, ram_code (the part of code copied to RAM and run
# there, which takes RAM as data does).
write_size() {
    sym() { nm "$1" | awk -v s="$2" '$3 == s { print $1 }'; }

    irq=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __irq_stack_top)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_limit)") ))
